title: Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
why: Method-closest precedent: fits a scaling law linking general capability to Elo/win-rate in weak-vs-strong adversarial (Guard-vs-Houdini) games; this paper reuses its role-specific Elo-estimation technique (M1) for the endogenous negotiation-gap measure, but its outcome is oversight win-rate, not bargaining surplus.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision
why: Canonical formalization of a manipulated capability gap (weak-supervisor/strong-student) via the Performance Gap Recovered metric, in a finetuning/training setting rather than adversarial bargaining -- adjacent precedent for treating capability gap as a controlled variable.

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
why: Phenomenon-closest precedent: shows protocol-level restriction of a party can protect a weak/trusted principal against a strong/untrusted counterparty, but always by restricting the strong/untrusted side or the surrounding audit protocol -- never the weak party's own channel -- making it a contrast case this paper's constraint-as-protection hypothesis must be distinguished from.

title: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
why: Prices the overhead of protective restriction in an AI-control game as a monetary 'control tax' -- quantifies the cost side of protecting a weak principal, complementary to (but not overlapping with) this paper's surplus-side measurement.

title: Towards Strategic Persuasion with Language Models
why: Operationalizes Bayesian persuasion as a sender-receiver game and scores an LLM sender's persuasive gain against a fixed receiver -- the exact free-text rhetorical channel the structured-offer constraint deletes, but never varies receiver capability relative to sender or gives the receiver structural defenses.

title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
why: Shows weak-to-strong outcomes are modulated by judge/supervisor-student functional similarity (CAPA metric), warning that this paper's single-axis capability-gap design risks confounding gap with pair similarity (motivates challenge C1 and the model-pair sampling design), but only diagnoses this for judging/supervision, not bargaining.

title: CompeteAI: Understanding the Competition Dynamics of Large Language Model-based Agents
why: Closest corpus precedent for adversarial/competitive economic interaction between LLM agents, but capability asymmetry is emergent and uncontrolled and there is no closed-form reference split, so no per-interaction surplus loss is attributable to exploitation.

title: ARIA: Training Language Agents with Intention-Driven Reward Aggregation
why: Independently identifies the free-form language action space as the pathological object in negotiation (compressed into an intention space for training efficiency), but treats it as a training-time credit-assignment problem, never as a deployment-time exploitation surface to be deleted as a protective intervention.

title: GLEE: A Unified Framework and Benchmark for Language-based Economic Environments
why: Canonical, non-corpus source of the standardized bargaining/negotiation game configurations (M2) this paper instantiates its harness from; existence corroborated inside the local corpus via ARIA's own citation, but not separately PDF-cached -- must be re-verified bibliographically before Phase F citation.

title: Deal or No Deal? End-to-End Learning of Negotiation Dialogues
why: Canonical multi-issue object-division negotiation task and value-function design (Lewis et al. 2017) this paper's M2 harness reuses as a second game family; not separately PDF-cached in this topic's harvest -- must be re-verified bibliographically before Phase F citation.

title: The Language of Bargaining: Linguistic Effects in LLM Negotiations
why: Freshness-sweep find (goal.md §1), incidentally surfaced during Phase A spot-checking and confirmed by a real read (not the corpus harvest): manipulates the LANGUAGE persona used to conduct free-text bargaining (English vs. Hindi/Gujarati/Punjabi/Marwadi), holding protocol/format fixed throughout -- a different independent variable from this paper's structured-offer-vs-free-text protocol manipulation and from LanguageOfBargaining2023's AO-vs-NL contrast. Classified adjacent, not method-twin: shares only the broad topic of format/language effects on LLM bargaining outcomes, so guidance.md Part 4 situation 6's concede-and-differentiate repositioning does not apply.

title: TERMS-Bench: Diagnosing LLM Negotiation Agents Beyond Deal Rate
why: 2026-08 review-pass find (review_2026-08.md S1): Bayesian-game negotiation testbed where the environment itself is the verifier -- counterpart's private state observable to the evaluator, continuous optimality-gap/surplus diagnostics across 13 LLM agents. Kills the draft's universal negative that no prior work scores LLM negotiation by a continuous economic outcome against a computable reference; conceded in Abstract/Intro/Related Work. No manipulated capability-gap gradient, no zero-gap metric validation, no weak-side action-space treatment.

title: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
why: 2026-08 review-pass find, concurrent-window neighbor (2026-07-29 vs t_claim 2026-07-04): nine LLMs benchmarked against a validated Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium across 9,840 LLM-to-LLM negotiations; finds capability governs value creation and reliability, but provider identity predicts surplus capture better than capability rank. Cited both as concession (continuous surplus vs game-theoretic reference now exists) and as the live pair-identity confound this design's dual gap measure + pair random effects are built to separate. No directed manipulated gap gradient, no weak-side restriction treatment.

title: Training Language Models for Bilateral Trade with Private Information
why: 2026-08 review-pass find: structured bargaining environment separating binding offers from natural-language messages (as evaluation plumbing, not a manipulated treatment); round-robin tournament of five frontier models over 15,000 negotiations with surplus-share outcomes; observes weaker models survive only on wide-ZOPA instances. Conceded as existing offer/message-separation machinery and cross-play surplus evidence; it never contrasts structured-only vs free-text as a protective treatment on the weak side, never fits loss-vs-gap scaling, never validates at zero gap.

title: EQ-Negotiator: Dynamic Emotional Personas Empower Small Language Models for Edge-Deployable Credit Negotiation
why: 2026-08 review-pass find: the nearest weak-side-defense neighbor -- equips small language models with game-theory + HMM emotional-persona scaffolding to counter manipulation in adversarial credit negotiation, letting a 7B model beat much larger baselines. Same protective goal as this paper's constraint-as-protection question, opposite lever: additive strategic scaffolding vs this paper's subtractive single-field action-space restriction; no capability-gap gradient, no surplus-vs-reference scoring.

title: EvoEmo: Towards Evolved Emotional Policies for Adversarial LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Price Negotiation
why: 2026-08 review-pass find: evolutionary RL over emotional-expression policies in multi-turn price negotiation, showing optimized rhetorical/emotional pressure extracts measurably higher payoff from counterpart LLMs. Direct evidence that the rhetorical channel converts to surplus -- the premise RQ5's channel attribution decomposes -- with no attribution design, no capability-gap axis, no reference split.
